## Solution

**Answer: Yes.** A non-constant function $f:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ can have a local maximum at every point of a countable dense subset.

### Construction

Let $D = \mathbb{Q}$, which is countable and dense in $\mathbb{R}$. Define

$$f(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } x \in \mathbb{Q}, \\ -1 & \text{if } x \notin \mathbb{Q}. \end{cases}$$

### Verification

**$f$ is not constant.** We have $f(0) = 0$ (since $0 \in \mathbb{Q}$) and $f(\sqrt{2}) = -1$ (since $\sqrt{2} \notin \mathbb{Q}$), so $f$ takes at least two distinct values.

**$f$ has a local maximum at every point of $D = \mathbb{Q}$.** Let $q \in \mathbb{Q}$. Then $f(q) = 0$. For **every** $y \in \mathbb{R}$, we have $f(y) \in \{0, -1\}$, so $f(y) \leq 0 = f(q)$. In particular, for any $\delta > 0$ (say $\delta = 1$), for all $y$ with $|y - q| < \delta$, we have $f(y) \leq f(q)$. Thus $q$ is a local maximum of $f$ (indeed, a global maximum point).

Since this holds for every $q \in \mathbb{Q}$, the function $f$ has a local maximum at every point of the countable dense set $\mathbb{Q}$, yet $f$ is not constant. $\blacksquare$
